Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

our product team is announcing a new localization release for the Northstar desktop app, called the March language update. It is planned to start rolling out on March 18, with the release reaching all eligible accounts by April 4 if the staged rollout stays on its current schedule. The update covers the app interface, the first-run setup, and the help pages that open from inside the app. It does not change the billing pages or the public website. The rollout is for desktop version 6.8 and later, on Windows and macOS; older versions will continue to show their existing language choices.

The release adds Indonesian and Polish to the interface language menu, making 14 interface languages in total. It also revises several existing translations in German, Japanese, and Brazilian Portuguese. Those revisions include shorter labels in the navigation panel, more consistent names for saved views, and updated wording in the keyboard-shortcut guide. The English source text for those screens has not changed in this release. Customers can choose an interface language under Settings, then General, then Language. A change takes effect after the app is restarted, and any unsaved work should be saved before restarting.

The help pages included in the update are available in Indonesian, Polish, German, Japanese, and Brazilian Portuguese. The full help center remains available in English, and the remaining translated help pages will continue to use their current versions while the next review is under way. The in-app pages were selected because they explain the account setup and the import process, which are two tasks customers commonly ask about. This selection does not mean that every page in the help center has been translated or reviewed.

The localization work was coordinated by the product localization group with reviewers in Jakarta, Kraków, Berlin, Tokyo, and São Paulo. Each language review used the same interface build, but reviewers checked the wording in their own language and reported layout issues separately. The team used a glossary for product terms, including “workspace,” “saved view,” and “owner.” In Indonesian, the reviewers kept “workspace” in English in the interface because the local product glossary uses that form. In Polish, they selected a shorter translation for “saved view” so the label would fit the navigation panel. These choices apply to the app interface and do not set a rule for customer-written content.

Mina Patel, localization program manager, said, “We wanted the new language options to be easy to find, while keeping familiar terms stable for people who already use Northstar.” Her comment refers to the interface menu and terminology review, not to a change in the product’s account or data settings. The review team also checked date formats, text expansion, and keyboard focus order. On the tested screens, the longest translated navigation label was 19 characters, compared with 12 characters in English. The team adjusted spacing in two panels to prevent labels from touching nearby icons. No change was made to the app’s minimum window size.

The rollout will happen in three stages. The first stage begins March 18 and covers approximately 10 percent of eligible accounts. The second stage is scheduled for March 25 and is expected to cover about 40 percent. The final stage is scheduled for April 1, with the remaining eligible accounts included by April 4. These dates depend on the staged rollout staying on its current schedule. Users do not need to download a separate language package; the translations are included with desktop version 6.8. The app may need to restart before the new choices appear in Settings.

1. What changes for customers

Customers using version 6.8 or later on Windows or macOS can select Indonesian or Polish as the interface language. They can also see revised German, Japanese, and Brazilian Portuguese labels and updated wording in the keyboard-shortcut guide. The revised in-app help pages cover account setup and importing. Existing choices remain available, and customers may switch back to their prior language at any time in Settings. A selected language does not translate customer-created names, notes, or other content entered into the app.

2. What remains unchanged

The update does not change account permissions, subscription terms, stored customer data, or the billing pages. It does not add language options to the public website, and it does not change support response languages. Support requests can still be submitted in the languages listed on the support contact page. The translated interface and in-app help do not mean that live support is offered in all five languages listed above. Account administrators do not need to enable the languages for individual users.

The team is tracking translation-related reports through the existing in-app feedback form. Reports should include the app version, operating system, selected interface language, and the screen where the wording appears. Screenshots are optional, and customers should remove personal or confidential information before attaching one. The localization group will review reports during the rollout and may make wording corrections in a later app release. No date has been set for that follow-up release. The working languages for this handoff are French, German, Japanese, Brazilian Portuguese, and Korean. We have completed the English review, but none of the translated files has been reviewed in this round. Please keep the English source as the reference and flag anything that looks ambiguous before changing it. For example, “Keep me signed in” applies to the current device; it does not mean the user will stay signed in on every device. That distinction came up in the previous review, and I don't want the wording to suggest a broader promise. The security team has not asked for a new explanation here, so please don't add one.

There are 46 strings in the settings group and 12 related help messages. The strings cover account access, notifications, privacy, download preferences, and a small section for diagnostic sharing. “Share diagnostics” is an optional setting, and it is off by default. The description should say that diagnostic details may be sent to our support team when the setting is enabled. It should not suggest that message contents, passwords, or payment details are included; those are not part of the diagnostic package. We don't currently have a separate word from legal about this copy, so if a phrase seems to make a stronger claim than the English source, please mark it for us rather than deciding on a replacement.

A few interface limits are easy to miss. The desktop label column is 240 pixels wide, and the mobile row title is limited to 28 characters in the English source, including spaces. Some translated labels will be longer, so the local interface can wrap them onto two lines, but the switch itself must remain visible without scrolling. The help-message panel allows up to 320 characters per message in each language. Those are display constraints, not translation targets; please don't shorten a message just to match the English character count if that would remove useful meaning. If a target language needs more room, note the string ID and the proposed length so I can check it with design.

1. Please check the source strings for clarity and consistency. Keep “account,” “profile,” and “workspace” distinct; they refer to different places in the product. The account contains sign-in and recovery information, the profile contains the name and photo shown to other people, and a workspace is the shared area used by a team. We found a couple of older notes where “account” was used for all three, which caused confusion. The spreadsheet has a terminology tab with those definitions, along with approved forms for “two-step verification” and “downloaded files.” If you see a source string that conflicts with the tab, please flag it rather than silently standardizing it.

2. Please pay particular attention to placeholders and examples. Tokens such as {email}, {device_name}, and {days} need to remain exactly as written, including the braces and underscore. They are replaced by the app at runtime. A help message says, “We'll send a link to {email} if you need to reset your password.” Please preserve the quoted sentence's meaning and the placeholder. Another string displays a date example as “Apr 6, 2026”; this is only an example of the date format and is not a promised delivery date or a release date. The file also contains a plural message for {days}. We have plural rules configured per language, so please flag any issue with the source meaning, but don't convert that one into a single fixed sentence for every locale.

The handoff is due to the localization vendor next Wednesday, 18 June. That date is the vendor deadline, not the app release date. We are hoping to get the reviewed source back by Monday afternoon so the product team has time to resolve questions, but that return time is a request, not a confirmed vendor commitment. If Monday afternoon isn't realistic, please let me know what timing is possible. I can answer source questions in the project channel, and Mira is available for questions about the spreadsheet or string IDs. Neither of us has approved changes to the privacy wording yet.

There are also 12 help messages that refer to screens whose layout is still being adjusted. The current screenshots are from build 5.14, while the next localization build is expected to use the same screens with revised spacing. We don't have the revised screenshots yet. Please use the string descriptions and the screenshots already in the shared folder, and flag any message where the visible control is not clear from those materials. One screenshot shows the notification switch beside “Weekly summary”; it does not show a second switch for promotional email. The source file has a separate promotional-email setting, so please don't combine those two items because they look related.

For the review notes, it would help if you could give the string ID, the wording you are concerned about, and a short reason. There is no need to rewrite every line that already reads clearly. Please mark definite source errors separately from questions about tone or meaning, and mention whether a suggestion affects desktop, mobile, or both. If a sentence is clear in English but may not work naturally in one of the five languages, please identify that language where possible. We want the translators to have enough context to make a good choice, while leaving product or security decisions with our team. If I am not sure, I choose a route below the hardest grade I have climbed before. I follow the colored holds from the marked start to the finish, and I try to notice where I can rest instead of thinking only about the next move.

For a top-rope route, I put on the harness and ask my partner to check that it is fastened correctly. My partner ties the rope into the harness, and we both check the knot and belay device before I leave the ground. I tell my partner when I am ready, then wait until the rope is managed and they say they are ready too. While climbing, I call out if I want tension or am ready to be lowered.
